common_name: Romeo Echeveria (Deep Red Wax Agave Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Separate rooted offsets in spring and let cut surfaces callus for a day or two before setting into fast-draining, gritty succulent mix.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering only after the soil is completely dry. Unlike the green-and-red-tipped species form of agavoides already in this dataset, 'Romeo' saturates almost entirely into a deep brick-red to maroon across the whole leaf when given enough sun and cool temperatures, with only the leaf base staying greenish. It forms a compact, mostly solitary rosette of thick, pointed, rigid leaves with a sharp terminal spine, offsetting slowly compared to many echeveria cultivars. Bell-shaped red-and-yellow flowers appear on short stalks in spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Painted Echeveria (Red-Striped Olive-Green Branching Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or separated offsets in spring in sandy, well-drained soil; established plants tolerate light shade better than most echeverias in this collection.

directions: Plant in sandy, dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Native to the limestone hills of Oaxaca and Puebla, Mexico, nodulosa is unlike the other echeverias here in that it grows on visible, much-branched stems rather than a single low rosette, with each branch tip carrying a rosette of concave, dull apple-green leaves boldly marked with purplish-red streaks along the margins and down the center. In summer it sends up a tall, arching flower spike bearing pale yellow flowers marked with pink-red. The shrubby, branching habit and racing-stripe leaf pattern set it apart from the solid-colored rosettes elsewhere in the dataset.

common_name: Fire and Ice Echeveria (Frosted Blue-Green Rosette with Red Margins)

planting.note: Set rooted offsets into fast-draining mix in spring, giving plenty of room since mature rosettes spread up to 18 inches across.

directions: Grow in full sun in fast-draining succulent mix, keeping water out of the rosette to prevent rot. This selection of subrigida is among the largest-rosetted echeverias in the collection, with broad, smooth, spade-shaped blue-green leaves deeply channeled toward the tip, each one outlined in a sharply defined, narrow purple-red margin that gives the cultivar its name. Heavy, upright flower stalks in late spring to midsummer carry coral-pink, orange-throated bells. The scale and painted red edge distinguish it from every other echeveria already in this dataset.

common_name: Frank Reinelt Echeveria (Large Red-Margined Farina-Dusted Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Detach basal offsets once rooted and pot into gritty cactus-and-succulent mix in spring; this cultivar clumps readily and can be divided every couple of years.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-draining, mineral-heavy succulent soil. Bred by hybridizer Frank Reinelt from a cross of Echeveria agavoides 'Prolifera' and E. colorata, this cultivar grows a noticeably larger rosette than the standard agavoides already listed, with pointed dark green leaves dusted in silvery farina and edged in red-orange that flushes into sunrise tones of pink and orange under bright, cool conditions. It offsets at the base to form a spreading clump over time, unlike the more solitary-growing agavoides species form. Arching stalks of pink-and-orange urn-shaped flowers appear in spring.

common_name: Pink Frills Echeveria (Ruffled Pink-Edged Mexican Hens Succulent)

planting.note: Separate and pot rooted offsets in spring into gritty, fast-draining mix; the pink margins and ruffling intensify with a full season of strong summer sun.

directions: Grow in full to mostly sun in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering thoroughly only after the mix is fully dry. Selected from Echeveria shaviana (Mexican Hens, already in this dataset), 'Pink Frills' shows noticeably brighter mauve-purple to silvery-blue leaf color and, more distinctively, a leaf margin that becomes visibly wavy and frilled with age and is edged in vivid pink, intensifying in strong summer light. Orange-pink bell-shaped flowers rise on arching stalks in summer. The pronounced ruffling and stronger pink coloring set it apart from the plainer species form.

common_name: Compton Carousel Echeveria (Cream-Variegated Blue-Green Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Pot rooted offsets in spring into gritty succulent mix and site with some midday shade, since the reduced chlorophyll in the variegated leaf margins scorches more readily than solid-green echeverias.

directions: Grow in bright light with protection from the most intense midday sun, in fast-draining succulent mix. A variegated selection from the secunda/imbricata hybrid group, 'Compton Carousel' forms tight rosettes of blue-grey leaves broadly margined in cream to yellow-white, with older leaves picking up a pink blush in winter; no two plants show quite the same marbling pattern, and it is notoriously slow and selective about where the variegation appears. This cream-edged, slower-growing habit distinguishes it clearly from the solid-colored echeverias already in the dataset. It has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

common_name: Blue Rose Echeveria (Classic Blue-Green Hen and Chicks Succulent)

planting.note: Divide off rooted chicks in spring and plant into fast-draining soil; this old hybrid tolerates cooler winter conditions better than most tender echeverias in the collection.

directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil; avoid letting water pool in the rosette. One of the oldest cultivated echeveria hybrids, dating to the 1870s cross of E. metallica and E. glauca, 'Blue Rose' forms tight, symmetrical, blue-grey-green rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves that flush pink at the margins in bright sun, and it offsets so freely that dense clusters of chicks form around the mother rosette faster than most other echeverias in this dataset. Red, bell-shaped, yellow-tipped flowers appear on branched, arching stalks in late spring and early summer. It is also notably cold-tolerant, surviving brief dips to near 20°F when kept dry.

common_name: Dwarf Echeveria (Miniature Teal-Blue Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Nestle separated offsets into shallow, fast-draining mix in spring; its tiny mature size makes it well suited to miniature dish gardens rather than open beds.

directions: Grow in full to bright partial sun in shallow, fast-draining succulent mix, letting the soil dry completely between waterings. Native to northeastern Mexico, minima is one of the smallest echeveria species in cultivation, forming tightly packed, artichoke-like rosettes only around 1.5 inches across in pale teal-blue with fine pink margins, far smaller in scale than any other echeveria already in the dataset. It readily clusters into a dense, low mound of miniature rosettes and produces yellow, bell-shaped flowers on short vertical stalks in spring. It has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

common_name: Argentine Echeveria (Large Pale Lime-Green Wavy Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root basal branches or offsets in spring in well-drained mix, allowing generous room since mature clusters spread well over a foot wide.

directions: Grow in bright light with some shade protection in well-drained succulent mix. Despite its trade name, this species is native to Mexico rather than Argentina, and it grows into a notably large rosette of broad, pale, almost translucent lime-green, wavy-edged paddle leaves that redden only at the tips under strong light. Over time it branches from a short stem to form sizeable multi-rosette clusters, distinguishing it by scale and pale color from every darker or bluer echeveria already in this dataset. Pink flowers appear on tall stalks in summer.

common_name: Flesh-Colored Echeveria (Grey-Purple Flat Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Separate rooted offsets in spring and pot into gritty, well-drained mix in bright light to develop the species' characteristic muted flesh-toned color.

directions: Plant in full sun to bright light in well-drained succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out fully. Endemic to Veracruz, Mexico, carnicolor forms unusually flat, open rosettes of narrow, pointed, glaucous leaves in a muted, flesh-pink-to-purple-green tone that gives the species its name, a subtler and flatter form than the more upright or brightly saturated echeverias already in this dataset. Showy red-and-orange flowers rise on arching stalks in the growing season, drawing attention away from the understated foliage color.

common_name: Letizia Sedeveria (Branching Red-Margined Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained succulent mix; as a hybrid it will not come true from seed, so propagation is strictly vegetative.

directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining, gritty mix, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings. An intergeneric hybrid of Sedum cuspidatum and Echeveria setosa var. ciliata, 'Letizia' grows in a noticeably more upright, branching, clumping-stem habit than the compact, low-offsetting Blue Elf sedeveria already in the dataset. Its small rosettes are made up of fine-haired green leaves that sharpen to red along the margins and keel in strong sun, and scorpioid clusters of small white flowers rise from the rosettes in spring.

common_name: Fanfare Sedeveria (Slender Blue-Green Farina-Coated Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Detach and pot offsets in spring in gritty, fast-draining mix; this hybrid offsets freely and fills a small pot into a tidy clump within a season or two.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright light in very well-drained succulent mix, watering thoroughly then letting the mix dry out completely before watering again. A Sedum x Echeveria hybrid, 'Fanfare' forms dense, stemmed rosettes of slender, pointed, blue-green leaves under a matte, powdery farina coating, more slender-leaved and compact than the rounder-leaved Blue Elf sedeveria already listed. It is a vigorous offsetter that builds into a low, spreading clump only 4 to 5 inches across, and produces clusters of yellow bell-shaped flowers in summer that are often reluctant to open fully.

common_name: Jet Beads Sedeveria (Bronze-Black Bead-Leaved Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining mix; cooler temperatures and bright light deepen the near-black leaf color.

directions: Grow in bright, full sun in fast-draining succulent mix, watering only after the soil has dried completely. Bred by Dick Wright from a cross of Sedum stahlii and Echeveria affinis, 'Jet Beads' has short, semi-upright stems densely strung with plump, pointed, bead-like leaves that shift from deep green to bronze, burgundy, and nearly jet-black under bright, cool conditions, a coloration and leaf shape unlike any other sedeveria already in this dataset. Small, star-shaped yellow flowers appear along the stems in summer.

common_name: Super Donkey Tail (Harry Butterfield Sedeveria)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring and grow on in a hanging container, since the trailing stems become brittle and easily broken as they lengthen with age.

directions: Grow in bright shade to mostly sun in very well-drained succulent mix, watering only occasionally and letting the mix dry out fully between waterings. Bred by Dick Wright from Sedum morganianum crossed with Echeveria derenbergii, this hybrid produces cascading stems densely packed with plump, teardrop-shaped, powder-coated mint-green leaves, growing noticeably larger and more robust than its donkey-tail sedum parent. Clusters of tubular coral (occasionally pale yellow) flowers form at the stem tips. Its long trailing habit sets it apart from the low, mounding sedeverias already in this dataset and makes it best suited to a hanging basket.

common_name: Jewel-Leaf Plant (Rose-Grey Chunky Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root leaf cuttings or offset rosettes in spring in gritty, porous mix; older stems tend to lean or trail and can be cut back and re-rooted to renew a compact rosette.

directions: Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil, watering regularly through summer but only sparingly in winter. Native to rocky cliffs of Sinaloa, Durango, Zacatecas, and Jalisco, Mexico, this species produces thick, chunky, rounded leaves that emerge rose-pink and fade to a powdery grey as they mature, clustered in rosettes atop erect-to-pendent stems. The rounded, gem-like leaf shape and pink-to-grey color shift distinguish it clearly from the pointed, pale-lavender leaves of Graptopetalum paraguayense already in this dataset. Small, pale yellow, star-shaped flowers open in spring and summer.

common_name: Chihuahua Flower (Flat Grey-Green Rosette with Magenta Blooms)

planting.note: Divide off clustered rosettes in spring into light, porous, well-drained soil, and give a little more shade than most graptopetalums since this species naturally grows near cliff faces.

directions: Grow in bright light with some shade in light, porous, well-drained soil. Discovered on cliffs in Chihuahua and Sonora, Mexico (and long sold under the synonym Tacitus bellus), this slow-clustering species forms nearly flat, ground-hugging rosettes of grey-green leaves, a quite different growth habit from the trailing, erect-stemmed Graptopetalum paraguayense already in the dataset. Its standout feature is a short flower stalk topped with strikingly large, deep pink to red, star-shaped blooms with dark pink stamens, among the showiest flowers of any small succulent in this group. It has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

common_name: Thread-Leaf Graptopetalum (Grey-Green Rosette with Bristle-Tipped Leaves)

planting.note: Separate offset rosettes in spring into gritty, well-drained soil; this high-elevation species tolerates drier, cooler conditions than many succulents in this collection.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright shade in gritty, well-drained soil, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings. Native to rocky habitat in Chihuahua, Mexico, at elevations over 7,000 feet, this species forms tight, nearly flat rosettes of 75 to 100 densely packed, metallic grey-green leaves, each tipped with a distinctive long, thread-like, reddish-brown bristle that gives the species its name and its finely textured, almost furry-edged silhouette. White flowers marked with dark brownish-red blotches appear in late spring, and the bristle-tipped leaves set it apart from every other graptopetalum already in the dataset.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online

common_name: Beautiful Graptopetalum (Blush Lavender Shrubby Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root leaf cuttings or offset rosettes in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; the branching stems benefit from occasional pinching to keep the clump full rather than leggy.

directions: Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil, watering regularly through summer and sparingly in winter. Native to Jalisco, Mexico, and formerly classified as Graptopetalum pentandrum subsp. superbum, this species forms nearly flat rosettes of heavily farina-coated, blush-to-lavender leaves at the tips of semi-decumbent, branching stems that build into a shrubby clump, distinct from both the trailing G. paraguayense and the chunkier-leaved G. amethystinum already in this dataset. Yellow flowers with red stamens bloom from late winter into spring.

common_name: Little Jewel Pachyphytum (Dense Violet-Tinged Bead-Leaved Succulent)

planting.note: Divide basally branched offsets in spring into fast-draining succulent mix; this species stays more compact than most pachyphytums, making it well suited to small pots.

directions: Grow in full to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried completely. Native to Hidalgo, Mexico, this species forms crowded rosettes of 30 to 80 short, thick, tubular leaves pressed tightly against each other, leaving angular facets on their upper surfaces where neighboring leaves press in, a faceted, jewel-like texture quite different from the smooth, egg-shaped leaves of Pachyphytum oviferum already in the dataset. The matted green leaves flush violet under stress or bright light, and barrel-shaped red-orange flowers with dark green or violet tips rise on tall stalks in late spring.

common_name: Hooker's Pachyphytum (Elongated Coral-Tipped Trailing Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining mix; long stems eventually trail and are best supported or grown in a raised or hanging container.

directions: Grow in full sun in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, soaking thoroughly then letting the soil dry fully before watering again. Native to rock cliffs from San Luis Potosi through Aguascalientes and Guanajuato to Jalisco, Mexico, at elevations over 6,500 feet, this species is unlike the compact rosette forms of moonstones already in the dataset: it grows on long, spindle-leaved stems that can reach 2 feet, at first clustered into rosettes but becoming more widely spaced along the stem with age. Leaf tips blush coral-red under strong light, and small, deep pink, bell-shaped flowers appear on the upper stems.

common_name: Werdermann's Pachyphytum (Thick Purple-Green Star-Leaved Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or short stem cuttings in spring in a lean, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix blended with extra grit or perlite for drainage.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright light in free-draining succulent mix, watering thoroughly then letting the soil dry out completely before the next watering. Native to the mountains of Tamaulipas, Mexico, this small shrubby succulent forms thick, almond-shaped, pebble-like leaves of star-shaped cross-section that shift from green to purple-toned, arranged in a looser, less tightly tiered rosette than the other pachyphytums already in the dataset. Bell-shaped flowers ranging from greenish-white to dark red hang from slender, spike-like stems above the foliage.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online
